title: Boss: The Salesman
concept: After this one you can find the sting in a sales line and answer both of its targets from the Pilot.
bookIdea: An angular transaction involves three ego states. The top message goes Adult to Adult, while the hidden message goes from the salesman's Adult to the buyer's Child, and the Child's reply decides the sale.

opener.setting: Sunday, 14:50, The Corner Table, the back room. Two tables pushed together, with a phone in its box on the cloth and the tea gone cold.

lines.text: “Right. For the exercise, I'm the salesman. This one is better, but you can't afford it.”
lines.cue: tapping the box, deadpan, the grin not reaching her eyes

opener.ask: Can you answer from the Pilot at both levels, three times in a row, when the salesman praises the phone and the sting is aimed at you?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: How this one works: most sales lines here have two targets. The top message goes to your Pilot, and the sting goes to another voice. Tap the voice the sting goes to, or say there is none.

items.text: “This one is better, sir. You can't afford it, but it is better.”
items.cue: pleasant, polishing the box with his sleeve
options: The Pilot, the part that checks the facts
The Kid, the part that wants and worries
The Boss, the part that makes the rules
items.why: The top line is a comparison, and it goes to your Pilot. The sting, you can't afford it, goes past the Pilot to the Kid, who hears it as a dare.

traps.0: The Pilot is where the top line lands, the camera and the screen. The sting is aimed somewhere else, so the Pilot is only half the target.
traps.2: The Boss would turn it into a rule, such as always save first. The line gives no rule, so the Boss is not where the sting goes.

items.example:
A school fundraiser, a parent who says: “This stall is the better one, but I doubt you can manage a stall like that.”
The stall is the top line, and the doubt is aimed at whoever has to pay.

items.who: Salesman, by the phone in its box
items.text: “This one has the better camera. It costs more each month, and here are both prices.”
items.cue: laying two price cards side by side on the counter
options: Nowhere. It is all facts for the Pilot
The Kid, the part that wants to prove itself
The Boss, the part that makes the rules
items.why: Both messages are plain facts, and they go to the same voice, your Pilot. With nothing aimed at the Kid there is no second target, so there is no sting. This is an ordinary matched volley waiting for your reply.

traps.1: The Kid would be the target if the line dared you or flattered you. This one only gives facts to compare, so there is nothing for the Kid to hear.
traps.2: The Boss would be the target if the line gave a rule or a verdict. It gives prices, so there is no rule in it.

items.example:
A cinema box office, a clerk who says: “The front rows are cheaper, the back rows have the better view. Here are both prices.”
Facts for the Pilot, and nothing aimed anywhere else.

items.text: “Most people who ask about the price end up taking the cheap one. You don't seem like most people.”
items.cue: leaning on the counter, already smiling
options: The Boss, the part that makes the rules
The Pilot, the part that is weighing the costs
The Kid, the part that wants to prove itself
items.why: The first sentence is a remark about what most people do, which looks like a fact for the Pilot. The sting is the second sentence, you are not like most people, and it goes past the Pilot to the Kid, who wants to show it is better than that.

traps.0: The Boss would take a rule or a verdict about what you ought to do. The line gives no rule, only a flattering comparison.
traps.1: The Pilot is where the first sentence lands. The sting is the second sentence, which asks you to prove you are different, and that goes to the Kid.

items.example:
A tailor's shop, an assistant who says: “Most people settle for the ready-made suit. You don't look like most people.”
The remark about most people is the top line, and the pride is what the line is reaching for.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Now you answer, and the salesman is pushing hard. Each reply has to answer the top line and the sting. Choose the reply that does both from the Pilot.

items.text: “The bigger one is for people who already know what they want. You look like you do.”
items.cue: tapping the screen with one finger, pleasant
options: I know what I want, and I want the price before the screen.
Sure, the bigger one, since I look like I know what I want.
I'm not sure I know what I want, so you choose.
items.why: Your reply owns the want, which answers the top line from the Pilot. Then it asks for the price before the screen, which answers the sting. A compliment cannot sell you a phone once you have asked for the number.

traps.1: That takes the bait. The sting is a compliment about knowing what you want, and this reply proves it by buying the bigger phone, so the Kid is the one who decides.
traps.2: Handing the choice over is a Kid move, and it makes the salesman the one who knows. The top line stays unanswered and the sting keeps running.

items.example:
A cricket club, a coach who says: “The senior team is for players who already know what they want. You look like you do.”
A plain reply is: “I know what I want, and I want the fixtures first.” It answers the compliment with a request.

items.title: Sunday, 15:05, The Corner Table, the back room
items.setting: Nadia is sitting behind a phone in its box, with a price card face down. She has said she is the salesman for the exercise, and she will not take the job seriously unless you do.

beats.text: “This one is better, you'll see the camera at once. But you can't afford it, not with your rent.”
beats.cue: turning the box so you see the price, not the phone

lines.text: “The camera is better, I can see that. The price is my call, so tell me what the cheaper one costs.”
lines.outcome: Nadia turns the box round. “Fair. Here's the cheaper one.” The rent comment has nothing left to grip.
lines.why: You took the camera as a fact you could check and the rent as a comment you could answer, so each target got its own reply from the Pilot.

lines.text: “Fine. Show me the cheaper one, then.”
lines.outcome: A second box is slid across. “Here,” she says, not warmly.
lines.why: You moved on without naming the sting, so the rent comment stays in the room unanswered. Nothing harmful happened, but the Kid still heard it.

lines.text: “You're right, I can't afford it, so I'll take the big one to prove you wrong.”
lines.outcome: She has the card reader out before you finish. The form is already on the cloth.
lines.why: You answered the sting from the Kid and bought the phone to win an argument with it. That is a trap, and it ends the scene here.

beats.text: “Most people in your spot take the bigger one. It's the sensible choice, and the monthly bit is small.”
beats.cue: sliding a form across the cloth, smiling

lines.text: “Sensible for whom? Write me the monthly amount and the total, and I'll tell you what my month can take.”
lines.outcome: She writes both figures on the form and turns it round. “Okay. That's honest.” She does not smile this time.
lines.why: You asked whose sense it was, and you checked the top line against the numbers. Both targets got an answer from the Pilot.

lines.text: “Let me think about the bigger one.”
lines.outcome: The form stays on the cloth, and the pressure sits there and waits.
lines.why: Thinking is a Pilot move, but you did not say what you were thinking about, so the sting stays on the table with the form.

lines.text: “You're right, it's hard to say no to nice things. Let's just pick the one you like.”
lines.outcome: She smiles warmly and starts the bigger phone's paperwork. You feel looked after, and the bill is already on its way.
lines.why: It sounds kind, but you handed the decision to the salesman, so the sting keeps running. The kind tone is the trap, and it ends the scene here.

beats.text: “You don't have to decide now. But the offer ends at six, and the one before this one is already sold.”
beats.cue: glancing at the clock above the tea counter

lines.text: “Then I'll decide by six, in my own time, with my own figures. You can hold the box till then.”
lines.outcome: A sigh first, then “Fine, but I'm only holding it.” The deadline is hers, and the choice is still yours.
lines.why: You set your own deadline and kept the decision with the Pilot. A deadline from the other side only binds you once you accept it.

lines.outcome: A card with the offer printed on it is slid across, the ink already fading at the edge.
lines.why: It is harmless, but it leaves the six o'clock deadline unanswered, so the pressure keeps its shape.

lines.text: “Quick, then. Put the big one on the card before it's gone.”
lines.outcome: The card reader is already out. You are committed before the tea has cooled.
lines.why: You let the offer's clock make the choice, which is the Kid rushing for the exit. It ends the scene here.

beats.text: “You'd look good with it. Everyone at Halden has one already, you'd fit right in.”
beats.cue: an easy smile, the voice of a friend

lines.text: “Everyone at Halden might have one, but I'm asking about me. What does it cost me over a year?”
lines.outcome: Nadia laughs and does the sum on the back of the form. The total makes her put the pen down. “Right. That's a real year.”
lines.why: You treated the comparison as other people's business and asked about your own year. The phone stopped being a club you wanted to join.

lines.outcome: Pleased with the point, Nadia nods. “Exactly. So the bigger one.”
lines.why: You accepted being fitted into the crowd. It is harmless, but it gives her the point she came for.

beats.text: “I'm only trying to help you here. People get stuck on the small things, that's all.”
beats.cue: a hand on the box, eyes soft

lines.text: “I know you're trying to help, and I still want the total before I decide. Can you write it down?”
lines.outcome: She writes it in neat figures and turns the form round. “There. Happy?” The soft voice has nothing left to pull at.
lines.why: You thanked the help and kept your own request. A kind tone does not change the numbers, so you asked for the numbers.

lines.outcome: The form is tucked under the box with a nod. The pressure is folded up and waiting.
lines.why: Polite and harmless, but the total is still missing, so the help is still doing the choosing in the back of your head.

lines.text: “Then help me. Just put the bigger one on the card.”
lines.outcome: The card goes through with a beep. The scene is over before the tea is finished.
lines.why: You handed over the decision in the same breath as asking for help. That is a trap move, and it ends the scene here.

beats.text: “So. Do you want the better one, or the one you can afford?”
beats.cue: pen over the form, a little tired now

lines.text: “Neither, yet. I'll take the cheaper one with the review I read, and I'll tell you on Monday.”
lines.outcome: A sigh, then a smile. “Fair enough. Ring me on Monday.” The cheaper box goes into a bag.
lines.why: You turned down both of the choices she offered and kept your own, which is answering from the Pilot. You named the phone, the review and the day, so the sting had nothing to hold.

lines.outcome: The cheaper one is rung up without a word. You leave with the box under your arm and a small sting left on the cloth.
lines.why: Choosing the cheaper one is sound, but you did not say why, so the sting got the last word.

items.payoff: The card reader beeps. You go home with a phone you cannot afford, and the first bill is already on its way.

fallout.them: Nadia pushes the box aside. “Let's stop there. Come back when you want to talk about the camera.”
fallout.you: You go quiet and let her fill in the form. The exercise ends with the paperwork half done.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Read the sale back. Two questions about the salesman's line and your reply.

items.text: “This one is better, but you can't afford it. Which kind of line is that?”
items.cue: setting the box down, pen capped
options: Double-talk aimed at two different voices in you
A cut, where the reply comes from another voice
A matched volley, where both messages go to the same voice
items.why: The top line is about the phone and goes to your Pilot. The sting, you can't afford it, goes past the Pilot to the Kid. Two targets in one sentence means the Kid is the one that gets hit, and that is the one that decides what you buy.

traps.1: A cut would need the reply to come from a different voice than the one spoken to. The line itself has two targets, so a cut is what you might do afterwards, not what the salesman did.
traps.2: A matched volley would send both messages to one voice. This line splits between the Pilot and the Kid, so the matched volley does not fit.

items.example:
A housing society meeting, a member who says: “The new gym is the better one, but I doubt you can manage the fees.”
The gym is the top line, and the fees are the sting for whoever is in the room.

items.who: Nadia, with the price card face down
items.text: “Count the voices in the salesman's line. Then think back to the barn chat, where both people had a second chat going. How many voices are in play here?”
items.cue: holding up three fingers, then four
options: Four: both Pilots on top and both Kids underneath
Three: his Pilot and your Pilot on top, and your Kid underneath
Two: his Pilot and your Pilot, since the sting is never said out loud
items.why: The salesman speaks only as the Pilot, so he supplies one voice. On top his Pilot talks to your Pilot, and underneath the same line is aimed at your Kid. That is three voices, and the sale is made by the third one, whose answer is taken at face value as a sensible purchase. In the barn both people had a Kid chat going, which made four.

traps.0: Four voices means both sides have a hidden chat, as in the barn. The salesman is only working your Kid, so there is no Kid chat on his side, and the count is three.
traps.2: Not being said out loud does not remove the sting. It still reaches your Kid, which is why the third voice answers and the sale goes through.

items.example:
A market stall, a trader who says: “This rug is better, but I wouldn't suggest it to everyone.”
His Pilot and yours handle the rug. The flattery goes to your Kid. Three voices, with the sale decided by the third.

debrief.nadia: I was the salesman today, and I said so, which is the difference between a role and a trap. The top lines gave you facts and compliments, and the stings went to the part of you that wants to show it is as good as anyone. The replies that worked named the phone and asked for the number, and they kept the decision with you.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this an angular transaction: three ego states are at work. In Berne's sales example the salesman's Adult speaks to the buyer's Adult on the surface and aims the real message at her Child. The reply is taken at face value as an Adult purchase, so the transaction is complementary at both levels.

reflection.prompt: Think of a deal, a price or an offer this week that came with a sting. Which part of you did the sting go to, and what did you say that answered both parts?
